item.title: Influencer University
item.description:
Good morning! Want to be an influencer? While I don’t think I have the stamina, I love watching the vlogs.

My colleague spent time with Haley DeKreek, a junior at the University of Arizona and member of the Alpha Phi sorority, who has more than 45,000 TikTok followers. She’s part of a boom of sorority content known as #RushTok.

Her chosen career path? Influencing. She’s in good company. A recent survey found that nearly four in 10 Gen Z respondents said they would take a million social media followers over a steady 9-to-5 job.

In the days before a homecoming game, Haley’s schedule was packed as she went from beauty appointment to beauty appointment. “I love being a girl,” she said.

Go inside the life of a sorority influencer.

We’re also covering:

Data centers

The next James Bond

International students

What to discuss in class today.

1. A winter nightmare is looming in Ukraine. Russia has opened a bombing campaign that is intended to strip Kyiv and other cities of heat, running water and sanitation.

2. Did a routine router upgrade lead to a U.S. ground stop? Officials thought that a facility in Arkansas was remote enough that they could do the upgrade work without much harm. The underlying cause is unclear. Here’s what we know.

3. President Trump is expected to meet with Xi Jinping, China’s leader, this week. The fallout from the Nvidia scandal is hanging over the meeting.

4. Congress is debating a bill that would charge data centers billions. It could make it easier to build data centers for A.I., but those centers would have to pay extra for access to the electric grid.

5. Raye is the top Grammy nominee. She tied a record Beyoncé set at the 2025 ceremony for most nominations for a female artist. Here’s a list of the nominees.

6. The next James Bond is … Robert Pattinson. The English actor succeeds Daniel Craig to become the seventh person to play the superspy.

7. Look up tonight. The Leonids meteor shower is peaking. It’s best seen from the Northern Hemisphere.

The University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill’s chancellor tried to protect the school from the wrath of the Trump administration. Work on cancer, suicide, AIDS and coronaviruses was sacrificed anyway. Here’s how.

Trump administration policies appear to be scaring away international students for a second year. A survey released today found that new international student enrollment at American universities plunged by 15 percent.

Student loan caps are complicating the dreams of some aspiring doctors, who are entering medical school with limits on how much they can borrow.

A former student who was sexually assaulted at Texas Christian University is suing the school. She’s using an unusual legal strategy, claiming that the university violated a consumer protection law in another state.

Trisha Paytas spoke at Harvard Business School.

Joe Rogan weighed in on the midterms. After relative silence, Rogan said that Trump’s policies had lost “the podcast bros.”

Maybe it’s a flop? Maybelline debuted its first new tag line in more than three decades. Some. People. Are. Confused.

Billy Evans said he would do it all over again. Evans, the partner of Elizabeth Holmes, said in a CBS interview that he would “100 percent” make “You Can See Everything” once more. Here are five takeaways.

“S.N.L.” brought back Bowen Yang. He returned to play the former Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang in a cold open with a gaggle of tech giants. Read our recap.

AO3, the fan fiction site, is back. The archive was taken down more than two weeks ago in a “security incident,” leaving its 12 million users in shock.

Do this to get ahead.

Laugh at yourself. Experts say it could help other people feel more at ease around you.

Strengthen your muscles. I’m finally working out again, and I need to start lifting more weights. These five muscles are important to prioritize as you get older.

Make some cookies. These are the best ready-to-bake chocolate chip cookie doughs.

Thanks for hanging out with me this morning. This newsletter is powered by your submissions — tell us about your classes, questions, crushes, side hustles and obsessions here.

Also: Times access is free for half of all U.S. college students through their school. Tell your friends to check if their school provides free access.

And forward this to your roommate, professor, club president or T.A. See you tomorrow!

Want more of today’s top stories? Tune in to “The Headlines,” our podcast that includes top headlines and analysis.

Any tips or feedback? I’m all ears. Email me at extracredit@nytimes.com.

The editor of Extra Credit is Talya Minsberg. Harrison Hill and Hiroko Masuike were our photo editors.

item.title: Cornell President Vows Fraternity Review in Wake of No-Confidence Vote
item.description:
Cornell University’s president announced on Monday a review of the future of fraternity life on campus and the hiring of additional sexual assault support staff members as he appealed to a wary campus for their trust in the wake of a faculty vote of no-confidence in his leadership earlier this month.

Michael I. Kotlikoff, the president, also vowed in the campus message that he would “fundamentally change how we prevent and respond to sexual violence” as part of an effort to make certain that the sexual violence experienced by a former undergraduate known as Jane Doe would not happen again.

“Sexual violence can have no place at Cornell: not on our campus, not in our community, and not in our culture,” he said.

Dr. Kotlikoff has been under fire since the former undergraduate filed an explosive lawsuit in September alleging that Cornell, her sorority and a fraternity did not do enough to prevent or respond to a gang rape that she said she had experienced at a fraternity house in October 2024.

In addition to the faculty no confidence vote, tens of thousands of people have signed an alumni petition calling for more accountability among Cornell's leadership. The university’s board of trustees has reaffirmed its faith in Dr. Kotlikoff as recently as Nov. 6, and said he can make the changes needed to keep students safer.

Among the changes announced on Monday were several efforts that have been rolling out in recent weeks, such as a pilot program offering free late-night transportation to get students home safely on weekends, which the university plans to expand next semester.

The university will also announce a full review of its Greek system that “will consider the future of fraternities and sororities at Cornell,” he said. The university has already made the decision to bar parties at fraternity houses for the rest of the academic year.

To address frequent complaints that not enough is done to support survivors once they come forward, Cornell has hired a new victim’s advocate in its sexual harassment and assault prevention office, as well as a new case manager in its office of civil rights. The hiring of an additional case manager and two prevention specialists is underway, the announcement said.

Sexual assault survivors who seek a criminal investigation can now ask that the New York State Police handle their case, if they want to avoid the campus police at Cornell, which has been criticized for how it handled cases in the past. Survivors can also ask the Ithaca Police Department or the Tompkins County sheriff’s office to run the investigation, the university has previously said.

Cornell will also mandate more education about healthy sexual relationships and sexual assault. A new orientation program on the subject that has already started for new students will be rolled out to all undergraduates next semester, Dr. Kotlikoff said. And in cooperation with the faculty, Cornell will establish a new academic center at Cornell focused on research and education on the prevention of campus sexual assault.

Cornell also debuted a new score card on the progress and completion of reforms to end sexual violence that have already been pledged. The dashboard shows that only 1 of 25 initiatives have been completed: the agreement with the state police that they would investigate sexual assault cases, if a survivor wishes to go that route.

Of the 16 recommendations made by a task force on sexual assault in March 2026 in the wake of Jane Doe’s original report of a gang rape in 2024, none have been completed, the score card shows. Instead, 13 are marked “in progress” and three are marked “planned.”

Dr. Kotlikoff will address students at a community forum on Monday evening, and hold listening sessions throughout campus between Nov. 30 and Dec. 14. “These will be opportunities for open, frank, face-to-face conversations — and for advancing the work we can only do together,” he said.

In October 2024, the former undergraduate filed reports with the campus police and the university’s Title IX office alleging that she had been sexually assaulted by seven Chi Phi fraternity brothers. The district attorney chose not to bring criminal charges.

Two of the men were expelled after a lengthy investigation by Cornell, and two more were suspended, while others received lighter punishments. Jane Doe withdrew from school in the incident’s aftermath, and the fraternity was barred from campus. None of the men have admitted wrongdoing or been charged with a crime.

Iris Packman, one of the faculty sponsors of the no-confidence resolution, said that Monday’s announcement was evidence that a broad push for a reckoning from leaders on campus was already having results.

“The president’s message and stated commitment to change would not have come about without the tireless advocacy from undergraduate students, graduate workers, faculty and staff who are working to hold this administration accountable for the unconscionably high rates of sexual violence at Cornell,” she said.

item.title: Enrollment in N.Y.C. Schools Falls by 23,000, Continuing Years of Decline
item.description:
Enrollment in New York City’s public school system has fallen by 23,000 students from last school year, the city’s Department of Education said on Monday, deepening a multiyear slide that has steadily shrunk and reshaped the country’s largest school district.

There are now 766,900 students in kindergarten through 12th grade, a nearly 3 percent decline from the previous year and the largest year-over-year decrease in five years. During the past decade, the city’s schools have lost 200,000 students.

The steep decline started before the Covid-19 pandemic, accelerated in its early years and then briefly stabilized amid an influx of migrant families. Now it is deepening once again, driven by declining birthrates and families leaving the city, another example of the affordability crisis that Mayor Zohran Mamdani has staked his administration on addressing.

To confront the growing number of schools with dwindling enrollment, school leaders have suggested some closures, but just a few so far.

“This year’s enrollment data marks a continuation of an alarming trend that raises fundamental questions about affordability, New Yorkers’ ability to raise families here, and how we direct resources to give our kids the education they deserve,” said Mark Levine, the city comptroller.

School districts across the country have been losing students for years, a trend fueled by a two-decade decline in fertility rates in the United States that hit a record low in 2025. The prolonged contraction has upended public education nationwide, leaving behind half-empty schools and forcing painful budget cuts.

Almost no area — big or urban, small or suburban — has been spared. The Los Angeles public school system, the nation’s second largest, started this school year with 373,000 students, down about 50 percent from its peak more than two decades ago.

In New York City, the fertility rate in 2020 hit the lowest point since at least 1980, according to the most recent city records. In 2021, 2022 and 2023, fewer than 100,000 babies were born in the city for the first time since 1936 during the Great Depression.

The outflow is not expected to slow soon: Enrollment could fall by another 110,000 students by the 2034-35 school year, according to projections from the School Construction Authority, which builds and renovates the city’s public school facilities.

The new enrollment data does not include New York City’s charter schools or private schools. After years of rapid growth, charter school enrollment has slowed considerably, recently reaching 150,000 students. Another 200,000 students attend private schools, where enrollment has dropped by about 10 percent during the past decade.

Despite the yearslong loss of students, education leaders and elected officials have been reluctant to make major budget cuts or close schools. More than 250 campuses now enroll fewer than 200 students, leaving them with fewer course and extracurricular options than those at larger schools. At the same time, the Education Department’s budget, the largest of any city agency, has grown to $45 billion from $33 billion eight years ago.

City leaders believe that expanding free child care can help stem the flow of families out of New York City. More than 94,000 children are enrolled in pre-K and 3-K, and the Mamdani administration rolled out 2,000 2-K seats this year. Another 10,000 seats will be added next school year.

The schools chancellor, Kamar Samuels, has not laid out a plan for addressing the sharp declines, but he has mentioned the eventual need to merge or close schools. The Department of Education has proposed closing two small schools, which collectively enroll about 150 students, and relocating another. Administrators have been considering more sweeping changes for next year.

Keeping the smaller schools open comes with a cost: Since 2020, the city has spent $1.9 billion to maintain funding levels at schools that have lost students.

“We are running a school system that was designed for a much larger student body,” said Ana Champeny, the vice president for research of the nonpartisan Citizens Budget Commission. “The city really needs to adjust its policies to address this new reality and to right-size.”

item.title: Protesters at Rutgers Disrupt Speech by Former Trump Border Official
item.description:
Gregory Bovino, the former face of President Trump’s immigration crackdown, was briefly driven from a Rutgers University stage on Monday evening as demonstrators drowned him out during a campus forum.

Mr. Bovino had been invited to New Brunswick, N.J., by the Rutgers Republicans, a student club. Advocates for immigrants condemned the decision, and hundreds of protesters had gathered to express their disapproval an hour before Mr. Bovino was scheduled to speak at the Douglass Student Center on the main campus of Rutgers.

Four minutes after Mr. Bovino began to speak, before an audience of roughly 50, about a dozen spectators stood up and began to yell and point at him. Several stood on chairs and hurled expletives. A group rushed the stage and were stopped by officers from the Rutgers Police Department.

“You should be ashamed!” one demonstrator cried out.

The police officers held the demonstrators back and told them to leave, and they did. Jorge Torres, a community activist who has regularly attended protests in support of immigrants, waved goodbye as Bovino walked out a side door.

“You’re not welcome in New Jersey!” he said. “You’re not welcome anywhere!”

Mr. Bovino briefly left before returning and criticizing Gov. Mikie Sherrill, who had said earlier on Monday that she was deeply disappointed by his appearance at Rutgers.

“Giving him a platform is the wrong decision,” Ms. Sherrill said on X. “People can agree that border security is important and the need for immigration reform is urgent. They can also reject the cruel policies of officials like Greg Bovino that cost people their lives.”

The student club did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Monday.

Mr. Bovino responded to the jeers by telling his critics to “wake up.”

“What are illegal aliens doing to our country?” Mr. Bovino said. “Filling our jails, schools and hospitals?”

Mr. Bovino was a top Border Patrol leader for about three months, taking on the job of carrying out large-scale deportation operations far from the international borders of the United States. He was removed from the job in January at the height of intense bipartisan outcry after federal agents fatally shot two demonstrators in Minneapolis.

He joined the Border Patrol in 1996, holding field and administrative positions across the United States and leading operations in California, Louisiana and Nevada.

Mr. Bovino has long held hard-line views on immigration. He attempted to publish his own research paper claiming that foreigners, both documented and not, were engaged in a “large-scale” attack on America’s environment. He has called for amending immigration law so that the government could deport green-card holders for even low-level offenses such as illegal fishing.

He had been a midlevel Border Patrol official before the Trump administration catapulted him to a top rank. His fall came soon after.

Mr. Bovino’s chaotic crackdowns on migrants were legally contested, and the deaths of the two Minneapolis demonstrators, Renee Good, a stay-at-home mother, and Alex Pretti, a nurse, intensified calls for his ouster. The administration moved Mr. Bovino back to California, where he had served as sector chief.

In March, The New York Times reported that Mr. Bovino was under investigation by the U.S. Customs and Border Protection agency’s professional responsibility office because of a report that he mocked a federal prosecutor’s Jewish faith.

That same month, Mr. Bovino announced his retirement, ending his 30-year career with the Border Patrol. He has since made media appearances criticizing the federal government.

Megan Florance, a Rutgers spokeswoman, said that the university was “committed to protecting freedom of expression and maintaining a secure campus.”

“Recognized student organizations may invite speakers to campus, including those whose views are controversial or generate strong disagreement,” Ms. Florance said. “Providing space for a student-organized event does not constitute university endorsement.”

item.title: Does This Man Have a Right to the Data From His Own Brain?
item.description:
On a recent Thursday, J. Galen Buckwalter drove 15 minutes from his home to the California Institute of Technology, steered his wheelchair into a laboratory and, as he had twice a week for two years, plugged in his brain.

More precisely, he allowed a researcher to attach wires to three metal knobs screwed into his skull like a cyberpunk mohawk. The wires connect to six chips that were implanted in his brain during a seven-hour craniotomy. They record his neural signals — the firing of his brain when he thinks, speaks or moves — and transmit them to a computer to be analyzed.

“Check this out,” said the researcher, a Ph.D. student named Sean Darcy, pointing to three colored lines vibrating on a monitor.

“Where’s that?” Buckwalter said.

“Motor,” Darcy said — meaning the chip implanted in Buckwalter’s motor cortex.

“That’s nice,” Buckwalter said, admiring the image.

Those neural signals may prove to be hugely valuable. Already, brain-computer interfaces have enabled people with paralysis to fly drones and helped people who have lost the ability to speak to communicate — using just their thoughts. Eventually, researchers say, they could allow the regulation of emotions such as pain or fear; the instant transfer of knowledge, such as a new language; or the merging of human consciousness with artificial intelligence.

Buckwalter, 70, was almost totally paralyzed from the chest down after a diving accident in his teens. He signed up for the study, conducted jointly by Caltech and the University of Southern California, because he wanted to make life better for others like him.

Also, he was curious. After a distinguished career as a research scientist at U.S.C., he had developed the matching algorithms that powered eHarmony, the dating website. He later started companies that tried to use data to understand human psychology.

Now he had a chance to get an up-close, never-before-seen look at the brain’s limits and potential. He imagined what he could do with the information Caltech would collect: run new experiments, supercharge his companies, learn more about himself and human resilience.

But when he asked the researchers for access to the data — after the craniotomy, after weeks of recovery, after hours upon hours in the lab — they said no.

The output from his brain belonged to the researchers, they said, not to him.

Today, the argument over who controls some of the most intimate information about us — what we buy, where we travel, whom we text — has become familiar, even tired. But little has been said about brain data. That is largely because that data has seemed like the stuff of science fiction, accessible only to scientists armed with the most specialized technology.

But that is quickly changing. Researchers and private companies are exploring other applications of brain-computer interfaces, including wearable headsets and caps. Elon Musk has a company, Neuralink, that has already implanted more than a dozen people, and he has said he envisions a world where people can upgrade themselves by merging with computers. Someday, information about how we think, what we fear and the essence of who we are could be as accessible as our shopping history on Amazon.

Yet, at least for now, there are few rules in place for who controls it.

Every time Buckwalter went to Caltech, he passed down a hallway decorated with posters showing the lab’s research. Each was illustrated with colorful diagrams of the brain, with participants labeled by code name: P1, P2. As Buckwalter — P4 — passed each poster, he thought: “That’s my data, that’s my data, that’s my data.”

The question was whether he could get it back.

Buckwalter was 16 when he dived into a river near his hometown in rural Pennsylvania and was hauled out by a friend, never to walk again. Afterward, he spent six miserable months in a hospital for “crippled children,” as they were called then, where he said his pain went largely ignored. When he was released, he taught himself to push a manual wheelchair and to drive. He vowed to avoid ever feeling so helpless again.

It was that vow that led him, in January 2024, to get implanted. He had developed severe arthritis in his hips, and though he couldn’t feel the pain directly, the condition drove intense sweating and blood pressure that would suddenly shoot to 250. More and more, he needed help from his wife, Deborah, with daily tasks.

Buckwalter took pride in his accomplishments and loved his wife and stepchildren. But he’d also always believed that he had a right to end his life if he couldn’t enjoy it.

“Purpose and meaning are no joke, and I was losing it,” Buckwalter said, sitting in his lime-tree-lined backyard outside Los Angeles, where he likes to sunbathe because it helps the arthritis.

Then a colleague told him about the Caltech study. Researchers were teaching people with spinal cord injuries to control devices like robotic arms with their thoughts, and they needed more participants.

Deborah worried about the risks, but Buckwalter felt only excitement. He met with the researchers, who made clear that the implant would not lead to any physical improvements. There would be “no direct benefits to you,” according to an informed consent form he signed, other than the satisfaction of helping people with spinal cord injuries in the future.

Buckwalter, though, saw plenty of benefits. One of his companies studied how to build effective teams in the workplace, and he imagined how much insight actual brain data could provide. He had once examined how women’s brains changed during pregnancy, and he wondered how implants might change his own cognitive functioning. He envisioned sitting in on meetings with the researchers, dreaming up new experiments with them.

Buckwalter captured his excitement in a song he wrote for his longtime punk rock band, Siggy (a nod to Sigmund Freud). It was called “Wirehead.”

“I’m a Neuronaut/ I am Wirehead / All hooked up,” he sang. “Humanity is destined to be digital.”

During the surgery, doctors shaved Buckwalter’s shoulder-length gray hair, cut open his skull and slipped the chips into his brain tissue. The first night of recovery was excruciating. Alone in intensive care, Buckwalter felt 16 again, back in the Pennsylvania hospital.

But the pain seemed worthwhile when Buckwalter’s new chips were plugged in for the first time. Sitting in front of an oversize monitor, with Deborah, his grandson and the researchers crowded around him, Buckwalter touched his own hand and watched neurons jump. Deborah touched his hand, and the neurons reacted differently.

By the end of the session, he could move a computer cursor with his thoughts. It’s happening, he thought in awe. So what can we do with this?

The root of Buckwalter’s fight for his brain data was the musical fungi.

Before his surgery, a friend had sent him a YouTube video about a musician who recorded electrical signals from mushrooms, then turned them into musical notes. If mushrooms could sound like that, Buckwalter wondered, what kind of music would his brain make?

Darcy, the Ph.D. student and a fellow musician, volunteered to help him find out. He wrote a computer program he and Buckwalter called NeuralNote that could translate the firing of Buckwalter’s neurons into sounds, with the pitch changing depending on the firing rate. When Buckwalter curled — or just imagined curling — his fingers, the neurons associated with that movement might fire faster, making the pitch rise. Extending his fingers might lower the pitch.

As with any instrument, it took practice to control it. Buckwalter then experimented with other movements, like wiggling his tongue. He found that trying to play two notes simultaneously was like patting his head while rubbing his belly. He and Darcy spent time after Buckwalter’s lab sessions, generating a whirlwind of beeps and whistles, Buckwalter’s eyes fixed with steely concentration on the monitor.

“Having the opportunity to learn how to play and integrate this new instrument into the broader field of music kinda makes me feel like Elvis,” he texted Darcy after one session.

Soon, he was imagining laying the brain recordings onto a song. But when he mentioned the idea during a session, one of the senior researchers said he couldn’t have them. He was taken aback; he hadn’t expected any resistance.

That afternoon, as Buckwalter drove past the university’s Spanish revival buildings, he asked Deborah: “What did we sign up for?”

The lead Caltech researcher, Richard Andersen, declined an interview request, saying he could not comment on individual participants.

Buckwalter’s surprise turned to anger. This wasn’t just about the music. As he saw it, blocking him from using and sharing his data was a disservice to the advancement of knowledge.

“My brain, my data!! Damn it,” Buckwalter texted a friend. But he didn’t know what he could do, so he just stewed.

A few months later, the researchers asked Buckwalter to sign a new consent form, updating the one he had signed before the study. It was presented as a formality, mainly changes to wording. But Buckwalter said he would not sign unless other changes were made, too.

In an email to Andersen last September, he outlined them. Participants should have the right to copy and commercialize their own data, he said, and the right to contribute data to other studies, if those uses didn’t interfere with Caltech’s. He also wanted to know whether the university was sharing his data with anyone else.

He knew he was taking a risk. If he didn’t sign the new form, Caltech could kick him out of the study — meaning that under the terms of the trial, he would need to undergo surgery, again, to have the chips removed.

“Participating in this project is one of the most satisfying experiences of my life,” he wrote, aiming to be cordial as he made his demands.

Months passed with no response from Andersen. Buckwalter kept attending sessions at Caltech, even though he hadn’t signed the form. In March, Siggy released a music video for “Wirehead,” featuring an animated version of Buckwalter in a baby pink suit with dozens of spikes protruding from his head. The song featured a sample of his neural notes that he managed to get on his own.

On March 31, Buckwalter was at home when he received an email from Andersen with the subject line, “New Informed Consent.” The attached form directly addressed the question of data ownership. But not in the way he’d hoped.

“You are giving your data to the investigators for this and future research, and the data will no longer belong to you,” it said. “If you have concerns,” the document continued, “you should not participate in this study.”

Buckwalter fired off an email to a lawyer who specialized in data privacy. “They have gone to extreme lengths to say they not only own the data, but they can do whatever they want with it,” he wrote. “If you have any ideas for how I should respond, please let me know.”

Buckwalter sat in front of his computer screen last month for a meeting of the B.C.I. Pioneers Coalition, roughly a dozen spinal cord injury survivors with brain implants.

They were discussing the feeling of seeing their own brains.

“You can prove to your buddies that always said you never had a brain — well, I got proof,” Buz Chmielewski said of sharing his surgery photos.

“My sister still says I Photoshop that — she still doesn’t believe me,” Scott Imrie chimed in. “Your little brother never has a brain, right?”

The Pioneers met monthly to share advice, support and, often, dark humor. (Vexatious bodily functions were a recurring theme.) But they also had a larger purpose: They wanted their voices heard, especially by the scientists and chip manufacturers who talked about brain implants but didn’t actually have one. At this meeting, they were discussing a draft manifesto about the rights of participants in brain-computer interface research.

The document, “Our B.C.I.,” had taken months to write and included topics like how the risks of trials should be explained and what was fair pay for participation. One point had been added at Buckwalter’s request: “Brain data should be understood as the participant’s personal information, with researchers as stewards of this information.”

Since receiving what Buckwalter called the “consent form from hell,” he had been busily consulting with lawyers, scientists and other patients. At neuroscience conferences, he buttonholed executives of companies working on brain-computer interface technology.

“I’m providing the raw material, and as a user, anything that comes from that needs to be done in a way that respects and honors who I am as a person,” he said onstage during a neuroethics panel at Stanford. He said he wanted to collaborate with researchers, not just be their subject. “The process is one of partnership. That’s what should be our North Star.”

The response was not always encouraging. In the United States, the law does not clearly define who owns the data in clinical trials, but university and government policies have generally granted control to institutions, not individuals. Institutions then lay out rules around access in their consent forms.

But there is no uniform standard for what the forms should say. As a result, they can vary greatly. Buckwalter learned from some of the Pioneers who were enrolled in other studies that they had no trouble getting their data. But if Caltech wanted to exclude its participants, it could.

“The law is pretty settled, I’d say, right now, and I think it’s settled in a problematic way,” said Francis Shen, a University of Minnesota law professor specializing in neuroscience who has called for giving research participants more rights.

Not everyone agreed with Buckwalter that he should own his data. One researcher observed that although the data came from participants’ brains, it required technology and time from others to extract.

Buckwalter stood firm. He still had not signed the revised consent form — let alone the “form from hell” — and he worried that pressure from Caltech would grow. So he found lawyers to represent him pro bono, and in October he sent a letter requesting a meeting with the institutional review boards of Caltech and U.S.C., which are responsible for protecting the rights of human participants.

On the Pioneers call, he shared that the universities seemed open to a discussion.

“That’s fantastic,” Ian Burkhart, the group’s founder, said.

“We just have to be real loud, right, Galen?” Imrie said.

“Exactly,” Buckwalter said. “At least listen to us. Maybe not act, but at least give us the time of day.”

Later that evening, he sat with Darcy in his backyard, plotting their next musical adventure. NeuralNote, the brain music program, had become a shared passion, and they often hung out outside of the lab to explore ideas.

Buckwalter was brimming with them. He wanted to try setting off his neurons in a fixed rhythm. Eventually, he wanted to make an entire album with his brain notes.

“Remember we tried the metronome?” Darcy said. “You got pretty synced up with it there toward the end.”

“I got ‘Jaws’ — doo-doo, doo-doo — I got that down,” Buckwalter said. “It’s a start.”

Their plans, though, would soon be put on hold.

In an email in late October, the chair of Caltech’s institutional review board, Ralph Adolphs, assured Buckwalter that Caltech and U.S.C. valued his participation in the trial and wanted to address his concerns.

But he also pointed out that Buckwalter had never signed the updated consent form. Caltech would have to pause his sessions at the lab until he signed it, or until they could agree on a new one.

“This pause is intended to protect your rights as a research participant,” Adolphs said. “It is not a penalty.”

In an interview, Adolphs said that Caltech wanted to find a way to share Buckwalter’s data with him, and eventually do the same for participants in all research studies.

Historically, he said, few people had asked for access, and Caltech had seen little reason to give it. There were too many risks: The data, once shared, could be leaked, misinterpreted or abused — by, say, health insurers to deny coverage. And the benefits to participants seemed minimal. Most would not know how to interpret such data (especially brain data, which Adolphs described as “a gigantic amount of numbers”).

But with A.I., participants might be able to get more use out of their brain data, even if the risks of abuse were growing, too. Researchers were also recognizing the importance of giving participants more respect.

“It is very likely that the past way in which these studies and their data were set up will change — the question is exactly in what way and how much,” Adolphs said.

There were still many issues to work out. The university had to decide, for example, what limits to put on the data, to make sure its scientists weren’t beaten to publishing their research. Caltech hoped to have a resolution, Adolphs said, “sometime in the coming year.”

Buckwalter hadn’t heard that directly. All he knew was that the hours he had spent in the lab each week were now empty. He was surprised by how sad he felt — he even missed the most tedious experiments, like repeating words until his eyes glazed over. Every day of waiting felt like a waste of everything he and his brain could be doing.

He decided to focus on what he could still do. In November, he and the other Pioneers published their recommendations on the rights of patients. He looked forward to speaking at a conference on neurotechnology in Washington, where he planned to make his case again.

That night in his backyard with Darcy, Buckwalter had reminded himself, yet again, why this all mattered. They were discussing the album of brain music, and Darcy suggested they also include guitar.

“It can’t be all experimental,” Darcy said. “We’ve got to get the average listener to listen in, too.”

Buckwalter insisted that it should be mostly neural notes. That was the whole point: “Nothing like it’s ever been done before.”

item.title: New Evidence Shows School Phone Bans Are Gradually Improving Test Scores
item.description:
School cellphone bans are beginning to modestly improve students’ academic performance, according to the first large national analysis that compared students’ test scores before and after the bans.

Schools with strict bans — requiring students to lock their phones in pouches all school day — saw math and reading scores improve as if students had an additional week or two of school a year, the study found. It was published Tuesday by the Center for Education Policy Research at Harvard.

U.S. students’ test scores began falling over a decade ago. The drop coincided with the rise of smartphones, raising questions about their role in the decline. The evidence so far on the academic effects of phone bans has been mixed. But the new study indicates they are starting to have an influence.

“The earlier studies on cellphone bans have been dismissed as implying small impacts, and in-school cellphone use has been ruled out as playing a big role in the decline,” said Thomas Kane, a professor at the Harvard Graduate School of Education and an author of the study. “But we think that’s mistaken.”

The study looked at 3.3 million students between 2021 and 2026. They were in third through 10th grade, attending 4,600 U.S. schools. Using scores on MAP tests, which track achievement from fall to spring, it compared the performance of students at schools that put in strict phone bans with those at similar schools that did not have such bans.

The annual gains reversed about half the annual loss that an average student experienced in the years leading up to the pandemic. (Students lost even more ground during pandemic closures.)

Two earlier studies reached mixed conclusions. One, of a single district in Florida in 2025, found small increases in test scores by the second year of the ban. Another, using schools’ average scores on a variety of standardized tests nationwide, found no statistically significant increase in scores.

The new study is different because it assesses individual students’ scores on the same test, looking at growth over the school year, across the country and through 2025-26.

The findings don’t necessarily contradict earlier ones, researchers on all three studies said. They all found small growth in at least some test scores — some more significant than others — and evidence that growth increases with time. That makes sense, they said, because just as declines added up gradually each year, improvement could also be gradual.

Brian A. Jacob, a professor at the University of Michigan and an author of the previous national phone ban study, said the new study showed effects “quite similar” to what his research team found. In his study, the positive effects were too small to be statistically significant, but in the new study, they weren’t.

He cautioned against being too optimistic about modest achievement gains, but added that “if they accumulate over time, year after year, that could be really important and really meaningful.”

Test scores in the United States, which had been increasing since 1990, began a sharp decline in the mid-2010s.

Researchers say there are probably several reasons, including the end of the federal school accountability law called No Child Left Behind, followed by pandemic school closures and an increase in absenteeism. The mass introduction of phones is another — by 2018, nearly all teenagers had one, and most said they used them daily at school.

Forty-six states now have school cellphone bans or restrictions. The rules are different among states, and schools also enforce them differently, which makes it hard to assess the effects. While some schools require students to lock away their phones, others let them keep phones with them, and some allow students to use them during lunch and between classes.

The study indicated that strict bans — physically restricting students from accessing their phones — had the largest effects on academic growth.

The gains were in both math and reading, for students at all levels of achievement. This surprised the researchers, who expected low performers to benefit most because achievement losses were largest among them.

“I think it’s really interesting and useful to know there’s no difference,” Professor Jacob said.

In reading, the bans also cut down on sliding backward — fewer students had their scores decrease over the year. Researchers say that reading seems to be more affected by screen use because it requires sustained focus, and because screens often displace time spent reading.

The study also looked at less rigid policies, like relying on students not to use phones during class. It found that these also led to academic gains, but the researchers said they were less confident in the results because the schools with and without these bans were different in other ways.

Banning phones probably won’t be enough on its own to turn around test scores. Research shows that successful schools do many interventions at once, and that execution matters. Still, even if the academic effects are modest, bans are an inexpensive solution.

The ubiquity of screens both in and out of classrooms could dilute the effect of phone bans. In interviews last year, several teachers said students had turned to their school-issued laptops to message one another or use the internet in class. Time spent on devices outside school could also be affecting student achievement, researchers hypothesized.

A major impact of phones “is almost certainly due to out-of-school use — the reduction in sleep quality, changes in mental health, distraction, displacement of time that might have been spent on homework,” said David Figlio, a professor at the University of Rochester and an author of the Florida study.

Teachers and researchers said test scores were only one potential benefit of cellphone bans. They could also improve student well-being, such as by decreasing cyberbullying, boosting social skills or encouraging engagement in class discussions.

The theory is that phone bans are not only “about instructional time, but about self-esteem and mental health and connectiveness to your peers,” said Sarah Novicoff, a research fellow on K-12 education at the Public Policy Institute of California. “Those are the questions I don’t think we know the answer to yet in the literature, and are important alongside test scores.”

Before Jill Anderson’s school banned devices, her third-grade students in Westchester County, N.Y., would text their parents during class, or phones would ring while she was teaching. Without them, she noticed benefits that went beyond academics: “When kids don’t have devices on them, they spend more time socializing, chatting, playing.”

item.title: Stolen Goods
item.description:
Good morning! I’ve had some packages stolen from my apartment building’s lobby. You, too?

We’re in good company if you have. An estimated 104 million packages were stolen in the U.S. in 2025, according to a report from SafeWise.

I reported on package thieves, known as porch pirates, nearly two years ago. One content creator told me that she moved to a building with a mailroom because she couldn’t deal with the stress of stolen packages.

My colleague Annemarie Conte at Wirecutter took it a step further. To thwart porch pirates, she became one. Read about Annemarie’s attempt.

We’re also covering:

A new video game

Babysitting dolphins

Fall wreaths

What to discuss in class today.

1. President Trump is in Asia. He was scheduled to attend a gathering with Southeast Asian leaders in Manila and then head to Shenzhen, China, where he’ll meet with Xi Jinping of China and Vladimir Putin of Russia. Read the latest.

2. Rich countries’ fiscal problems are affecting the world’s poorest countries. High interest rates and other global shocks have battered the economies of developing countries.

3. The Trump administration is investigating Megaspeed. The company was once led by Alice Huang, who U.S. officials believe worked as a Chinese intelligence asset while having an affair with Jensen Huang, the former chief executive of Nvidia.

4. A new trial date has been scheduled for Lindsay Clancy. The first trial for the deaths of her three young children ended with a deadlocked jury.

5. Grand Theft Auto VI is almost here. The newest installment of the video game franchise has already reached 15 million preorders, according to the data tracker Sensor Tower. It’s set to bring in billions.

What you’re wearing.

Kitty Edwards, 21, biology major at Wesleyan University

The outfit: Fashion is my hobby, so if I have the time, I’ll bedazzle myself. Some of my friends tell me they feel underdressed next to me, but I also have quite a few very fashionable friends. Also, as you can see, my backpack is very much her own thing. My outfits do not always go with her.

The occasion: To the library or some other study nook, where nobody will see me. I’m too busy to strut!

Anything else you’d like to share? People think I am a theater, art studio or English major. I engage with all three, as I am an illustrator, puppeteer/puppet designer, actor and creative writer, but I am actually a biology major.

Nobody guesses that, and quite frankly, I have met few fellow over-the-top-snazzy STEM majors.

Submit your outfits to Fit Check.

Michael Kotlikoff, the president of Cornell University, announced a planned review of the future of fraternity life on campus in the wake of a faculty vote of no confidence in his leadership.

The Supreme Court rejected a Trump administration request to bring back research grant cuts to the University of California system.

Protesters at Rutgers University disrupted a speech by Gregory Bovino, the former face of Trump’s immigration crackdown.

A student who had been accepted to Washington and Lee University’s law school, despite his expulsion from Tulane University for sexual assault, is no longer enrolled, according to The Washington Post. An investigation published on Monday by The Post found that the student received a diploma from Tulane while the school was investigating him for rape.

How do you maintain a masterpiece? Before retiring this year, Anny Aviram, a senior conservator, spent more than 50 years working at the Museum of Modern Art. She has touched paintings by Vincent van Gogh, Claude Monet and Jackson Pollock. The photos of her work are awesome.

Dolphin day care? It’s surprising scientists. Male Franciscana dolphins babysit, an extremely rare behavior for male mammals. Scientists are trying to figure out if they are thoughtful fathers or just hope to be.

Do this to get ahead.

Make a fall wreath. All those leaves and twigs on the ground don’t need to go to waste. This handmade decoration can brighten up a door or a holiday table. Here’s how to make one.

Watch “The Traitors.” The finale is this week. If you haven’t tuned in yet, the murder mystery game is also a great crash course in literature.

Do you know where these novels are set? They’re all on college campuses. Take our quiz.

Thanks for hanging out with me this morning. This newsletter is powered by your submissions — tell us about your classes, questions, crushes, side hustles and obsessions here.

Also: Times access is free for half of all U.S. college students through their school. Tell your friends to check if their school provides free access.

And forward this to your roommate, professor, club president or T.A. See you tomorrow!

Want more of today’s top stories? Tune in to “The Headlines,” our podcast that includes top headlines and analysis.

Any tips or feedback? I’m all ears. Email me at extracredit@nytimes.com.

item.title: Study Hard, Get a Career, Get Ahead? It’s Not What It Used to Be.
item.description:
Protest movements have long relied on students as some of the most ardent foot soldiers. Young people have been on the front lines of protests against war, climate change and racial inequality. But in huge protests that have shaken India and France this fall, students have revolted against the failed promises of education itself.

In India, students took to the streets after the government abruptly canceled the results of a medical-school admissions exam because test questions had been leaked online. Aspiring doctors had to take the test again, after many spent years studying for up to 12 hours a day in hopes of winning one of the coveted spots — and the chance of upward mobility. Young people across the country saw the scandal as emblematic of a broken education system and were furious.

In France, students in poor suburbs outside Paris began protesting the decrepit physical condition of their schools, an opaque university admissions system and absent teachers. French education had long promised to serve as a “social elevator” enabling young people to advance in society, but had fallen into disrepair. Soon, demonstrations spread across the country and, in some cities, spiraled into rioting.

In both countries, the anger of the students shows no signs of abating. And while in many ways France and India could hardly be more different, their unrest was sparked by a similar source of outrage: the breakdown of a foundational social contract that one could call the meritocratic bargain.

It is a promise that lies at the core of many countries’ political compacts. Though specifics can vary, the central proposition usually goes something like this: A fair society rewards merit. Educational achievements are a good measure of merit because education is open to all and leads to valuable skills. Therefore, education should be a route to social and economic advancement.

The value of this system is not just that it selects for those with high ability, but also that it offers a justification for the resulting socioeconomic hierarchy — including who ends up at the bottom. “All selection mechanisms generate losers,” said Nicholas Kuipers, a professor at Princeton University who studies the politics of meritocracy. “The question is, Who do you want to be a loser, and who do you want to be a winner?”

In many places around the world, that system has proved to be remarkably effective, in large part because education has translated relatively straightforwardly into economic mobility.

But increasingly, many who work hard at higher education, often going into debt and sacrificing years of earnings potential to do so, are finding that the rewards are not there at the end. Instead of expected winnings, many young people are greeted with a life of economic struggle.

This discontent is affecting politics elsewhere as well. In the United States, data from The New York Times showed that 70 percent of voters under 30 in the recent midterm elections cast their ballots for Democrats, who tapped educated young people’s widespread frustration over being saddled with debt and stuck in low-paid, dead-end jobs.

In Serbia, student protests grew into a political movement that ousted Aleksandar Vucic, the country’s longtime nationalist strongman, in an election last month. And young people across Europe are set to walk out on Nov. 20 in a general strike that could disrupt schools and businesses throughout the continent.

An even bigger threat looms on the horizon, one that could upend the bargain everywhere: A.I. promises to dramatically restructure, or perhaps sever completely, the relationship between education and well-paid work.

That has the potential to further challenge not only the distribution of economic rewards, but the political bargain on which modern societies have been built.

Historically, such moments have been explosive — even revolutionary.

The version of the meritocratic bargain we see today, with university education as a primary filter for middle-class careers, is a relatively recent construct, and not to be taken for granted.

Britain didn’t introduce universal, free secondary education until 1944. In the United States, college was largely the province of the privileged few until the G.I. Bill opened access to veterans after World War II. Around the same time, the SAT created the first nationally standardized benchmark for admissions.

In countries whose economies developed later, the bargain took even longer to take shape. In India, the national college entrance exam was not introduced until the 1960s. In China, there is a long history of using meritocratic exams to select civil servants and other elites, but that system was disrupted by 20th-century reforms and the Cultural Revolution. The modern system was ushered in by Deng Xiaoping. In 1977 he re-established the national “gaokao” exam system as part of a post-Cultural Revolution rebuilding process. In the late 1990s, further reforms radically expanded university access.

For individuals, this access to education promised more money, more status or both. But for governments, it also offered political stability — a way to convince people to buy into society as currently structured, by promising the potential for advancement to the underprivileged without ousting those who had wealth and power already.

The Times would like to hear about your experience as a federal worker under the second Trump administration. We may reach out about your submission, but we will not publish any part of your response without contacting you first.

Research has shown that the prospect of upward mobility — sometimes abbreviated as POUM — can make the poor less likely to demand redistribution. In China, merit-based selection for civil service jobs made people more willing to tolerate inequality, Hanzhang Liu, a political scientist at Florida State University, has found.

When people believed the system was meritocratic, they were more likely to attribute their failures to their own poor abilities, or to the high quality of the competition, she said. But when they did not believe so, those who lost out on jobs were more likely to consider the system rigged.

Still, education-based meritocracy puts significant burdens on the young people working to advance, and on their families. In India, students often go into debt and spend years of grueling study to try to win spots at the most prestigious engineering and medical programs.

In South Korea, national tests have generated an entire industry of cram schools known as hagwons, where students toil for hours each day on top of their regular schoolwork. In the United States, networks of charter schools like KIPP popularized the idea that for poor, ambitious kids, “college starts in kindergarten.” And when actual college starts, American students can easily take on six-figure debts for their degrees.

Just as the meritocratic bargain can be a source of social cohesion, a breakdown can become a trigger for social explosion.

In 1905, China abolished the national civil service exam that had for 1,300 years been a major way to recruit elites, including government bureaucrats. That move came as a shock to the people who had invested in years of education, hoping to earn a privileged position in society.

Those shattered expectations contributed to the revolutionary uprisings that eventually overthrew the imperial dynasty in 1911, according to the economists Ying Bai, at the University of Hong Kong, and Ruixue Jia, at the University of California, San Diego.

In an influential 2016 paper, they found that frustrated commoners who had hoped to become elites via the exam were especially likely to join the revolution. Disillusioned scholars flocked to revolutionary organizations in search of alternative routes to advancement, and became a major force behind the revolt.

That is not to say that France’s unrest signals the imminent return of the guillotine. But the recent protests there, and in other European countries like Italy and Spain, were fueled, in part, by the sense that the old order was enriching itself at the expense of providing opportunities for young people.

Much the same can be said of the student protest movement that led to the election defeat of Mr. Vucic in Serbia, where angry young people felt that meritocratic opportunity had been crowded out by corruption.

Protests can be a blunt instrument. But data show that the demonstrators have a point. In Europe, high unemployment rates for young people, paired with skyrocketing costs of living, have put the traditional milestones of independent adulthood out of reach for many.

Even in countries with healthier economies, there are signs that the breakdown of the meritocratic bargain is already having political consequences. In India, economic growth has been stronger, but it has not created enough jobs to keep up with the expansion of higher education.

In the United States, the emphasis on higher education as a sorting mechanism has led to people pouring tens of thousands of dollars into degrees that no longer necessarily confer economic advancement but still charge as if they do. Discontent has fueled the rise of political movements like the Democratic Socialists of America and efforts to unionize the work forces of companies like Starbucks and Amazon, Noam Scheiber, a Times labor reporter, writes in his new book, “Mutiny: The Rise and Revolt of the College-Educated Working Class.”

But the biggest blow to the meritocratic bargain may be yet to come, as many fear that A.I. could do for knowledge work what a meteor strike once did for the dinosaurs.

A.I.’s arrival has already wiped out some entry-level technical jobs. In the United States, young coders are finding themselves working at Chipotle rather than starting the highly paid tech careers they had expected.

Even if A.I. does not eliminate professionals like lawyers, scientists and doctors, it may radically reshape those fields — and perhaps slash the salaries that come with them.

Some professions may adapt by making greater use of A.I. tools, even as other careers see their pay and numbers collapse. With time, new educational structures may also develop to match skills and meritocratic selection to the demands of a new economy.

But such profound economic change is by its very nature disruptive. In the meantime, it is likely to sow even more confusion about how young people can set themselves up for success, or prevent themselves from sliding down the economic ladder.
